title: Ofcom Under Pressure: Regulating Online Safety
label: 15 September 2026 · Ofcom on the Online Safety Act
summary: This hearing examined how Ofcom is implementing the Online Safety Act, focusing on its slow progress, enforcement challenges, and the impact of new government plans like the social media ban for under-16s. The committee questioned Ofcom witnesses on whether the Act is making people safer, particularly children, and explored issues such as the safe harbour provision, enforcement powers, and the need for targeted reforms. The main conclusion was that while some changes are visible, the regime is still in its early days, and without additional powers and funding, Ofcom cannot fully deliver on its promises.

speakers.label: Mark Bunting
speakers.name: Mark Bunting
speakers.role: Director, Online Safety Strategy Delivery, Ofcom

chapters.title: Implementation Timeline
chapters.takeaway: The Online Safety Act is being rolled out in phases, with categorised services duties expected by mid-2027, but new government plans could cause delays.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Welcome. Could you introduce yourselves and explain which parts of the Online Safety Act are now in effect?

turns.speaker: Oliver Griffiths
turns.text: I'm Oliver Griffiths, group director for online safety at Ofcom. We're balancing three big pieces of work: implementing the Act, driving compliance, and preparing for the new social media ban.

turns.speaker: Mark Bunting
turns.text: I'm Mark Bunting, director of strategy delivery. The Act has three main planks: illegal harms, protecting children, and duties for categorised services. We've brought illegal harms and children's codes into force, but the categorised services part was delayed by a legal challenge.

turns.speaker: Mark Bunting
turns.text: We expect the categorised services duties to be fully in force by mid-2027, though that depends on ongoing talks with the government about sequencing and resources.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: What impact will the government's plan for a social media ban for under-16s have on your timetable?

turns.speaker: Oliver Griffiths
turns.text: We were already fully loaded, so we've had to move staff to work on the ban. Without extra funding, something would have to give. The government has promised extra money, and we're in detailed discussions. We think it's doable if it's resourced and sequenced right.

chapters.title: Lessons Learned and the Safe Harbour
chapters.takeaway: Ofcom has learned to engage stakeholders earlier, but the safe harbour provision in the Act can let companies off the hook even if risks remain.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: What lessons have you learned from implementing the first phases, and how are they shaping your approach to the new duties?

turns.speaker: Mark Bunting
turns.text: We learned that we need to engage more with industry and civil society before publishing proposals. The work on women and girls was more collaborative. Also, the safe harbour in the Act means if companies follow our codes, they're deemed compliant, even if risks remain. That can be limiting.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: The Children's Commissioner said she asked to see risk assessments but you refused. Can you explain?

turns.speaker: Oliver Griffiths
turns.text: We haven't received a formal request. Under Section 393, we need company consent to share risk assessments with third parties. If she makes a formal request, we'll ask the companies and follow that process.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: So if she asks formally, you'll facilitate it?

turns.speaker: Oliver Griffiths
turns.text: Absolutely, we'll go to the companies and check they're happy to share. We've had informal discussions for months.

chapters.title: Is the Act Making People Safer?
chapters.takeaway: Ofcom points to progress like age gates and geoblocking, but admits overall impact is underwhelming, especially on large services used by children.

turns.speaker: Lord Storey
turns.text: Has the Online Safety Act made children and adults in the UK safer online?

turns.speaker: Oliver Griffiths
turns.text: That's the fundamental question. We've seen big changes: 76% of companies surveyed completed risk assessments, and many big services like Reddit, X, and Discord have age gates. Porn sites have high age verification uptake. We've also seen geoblocking of harmful sites.

turns.speaker: Oliver Griffiths
turns.text: But we're underwhelmed by the overall effect so far, especially on large services most used by children. We've secured some commitments from X, Meta, and Snap, but it's a one-way ratchet that will build over time.

turns.speaker: Lord Storey
turns.text: The Children's Commissioner said the Act has made 'absolutely no difference'. How do you respond?

turns.speaker: Oliver Griffiths
turns.text: We share the frustration. We're trying to change corporate cultures built over decades. The Act drives change through risk assessments, not just content takedown. It takes time, but we're still early in the journey.

turns.speaker: Mark Bunting
turns.text: We've seen steps, but there's a long way to go. For example, some firms have made it harder for strangers to approach children, but they may not have good ways to identify who the children are. You can change one system but not the whole system.

turns.speaker: Lord Storey
turns.text: Should we allow tech companies to operate if they can't guarantee children's safety?

turns.speaker: Oliver Griffiths
turns.text: Society has said there's no freedom to operate in this space. The Act puts duties on companies. If they breach, we can enforce, and ultimately we can seek business disruption measures to stop their access to the UK.

chapters.title: Gaming and Proactive Tech
chapters.takeaway: Ofcom has focused on user interactions in gaming but lacks scope for broader issues like screen time; proactive tech could help but is limited by the Act.

turns.speaker: Baroness Caine of Kentish Town
turns.text: What progress have you made on gaming?

turns.speaker: Oliver Griffiths
turns.text: Some gaming services like Xbox and Steam have introduced age gates themselves. It's important, but not front and centre compared to social media and child protection.

turns.speaker: Mark Bunting
turns.text: We've focused on interactions between users, like on Roblox, where we have evidence of harm. Controls like age verification and preventing adults from approaching children have been effective. But broader issues like violence in games and screen time aren't captured by the Act.

turns.speaker: Baroness Fleet
turns.text: The Molly Rose Foundation says teenagers' exposure to suicide, self-harm, and eating disorder content has barely changed. What's stopping you going further faster?

turns.speaker: Mark Bunting
turns.text: We can require proactive monitoring tools to identify harmful content, but the Act sets high thresholds for accuracy and effectiveness due to privacy and free expression concerns. We're gathering evidence and consulting on wider use. We think these tools are key, but it's not clear the Act requires companies to use them.

turns.speaker: Baroness Fleet
turns.text: That seems like a fundamental flaw.

turns.speaker: Mark Bunting
turns.text: It's not a part of the legislation that's had much discussion. The tools are intrusive, but we think the case is strong. We'll have more to say after our consultation this autumn.

chapters.title: Enforcement and Perceptions
chapters.takeaway: Ofcom insists it is using its enforcement powers, but challenges like overseas services and unpaid fines limit its bite, and perceptions of slowness persist.

turns.speaker: Baroness Elliott of Whitburn Bay
turns.text: Stakeholders say Ofcom is slow and reactive. Why is it hard to respond quickly to new harms?

turns.speaker: Oliver Griffiths
turns.text: We moved quickly on Grok on X, launching an investigation within two weeks. We have 140 priority offences and constant dialogue with government. We're a repository for intelligence. But we're operating in a highly litigious environment—Meta has launched judicial reviews against us, and services are appealing our categorisation register.

turns.speaker: Baroness Elliott of Whitburn Bay
turns.text: Sir Jeremy Wright said he doesn't find in the Act support for the idea you have to know something will work before you try it. Is that your approach?

turns.speaker: Oliver Griffiths
turns.text: We have an open risk appetite on legal issues. But we need to balance risks. We don't want to get clobbered legally by deep-pocketed firms. We're learning as we go.

turns.speaker: Lord Kirkhope of Harrogate
turns.text: There's a perception you don't use your teeth. Is it legal constraints or reluctance?

turns.speaker: Suzanne Cater
turns.text: I agree we need to use our teeth. We have opened six enforcement programmes and 40 investigations, covering over 100 services. We've imposed £7 million in penalties. But some services are overseas with no UK assets, and some haven't paid fines. We're pursuing those.

turns.speaker: Suzanne Cater
turns.text: Business disruption measures are difficult because we can only apply if there's ongoing non-compliance. If a service withdraws from the UK or comes into compliance, we can't use them. It's frustrating.

turns.speaker: Viscount Colville of Culross
turns.text: On the suicide forum, should the Act be amended to force companies to deal with VPNs?

turns.speaker: Oliver Griffiths
turns.text: That's a political decision outside our remit. VPN use went up after age gates, but not massively. The government is considering recommendations. We'll do what we're told.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: How much of the £7 million in fines has been paid?

turns.speaker: Suzanne Cater
turns.text: I don't have the figure, but the majority hasn't been paid. We'll follow up.

turns.speaker: Oliver Griffiths
turns.text: As we move to bigger companies with UK assets, this will be less of an issue.

chapters.title: Legal Reforms and International Comparisons
chapters.takeaway: The Meta settlement in the US highlights gaps in the Act, such as algorithmic harm and screen time, but Ofcom is cautious about major changes.

turns.speaker: Lord Knight of Weymouth
turns.text: The Meta settlement in the US was eye-catching. Does it change how much you pursue in fines?

turns.speaker: Oliver Griffiths
turns.text: It changes the game by bringing safety to the boardroom. Our fines are capped at 10% of qualifying worldwide revenue. We won't be swayed by $18 billion. Also, fines go to the Treasury, not to us.

turns.speaker: Lord Knight of Weymouth
turns.text: The settlement was about system design, not just content. Is that instructive?

turns.speaker: Mark Bunting
turns.text: Much of it aligns with our codes, but it went further on features like screen time and addictive effects, which the Act didn't bring into scope. That's a judgment for Parliament.

turns.speaker: Lord Knight of Weymouth
turns.text: Should it be improved to include those?

turns.speaker: Mark Bunting
turns.text: That's for Government and Parliament. The Government has made commitments on curfews and time limits that go beyond current debate.

turns.speaker: Oliver Griffiths
turns.text: We don't have powers to enforce beyond the Act, but we encourage firms to go further. We'd like them to commit in the UK as they have elsewhere.

turns.speaker: Lord Knight of Weymouth
turns.text: Would pursuing platforms for recklessness be better than the codes and legal certainty?

turns.speaker: Oliver Griffiths
turns.text: We want change quickly, but we're in early days. Targeted interventions could improve things. The UK doesn't have the same culture of class actions. Putting duty on companies and incentivising them is a good principle.

chapters.title: Single Change and Closing
chapters.takeaway: Each witness suggests one reform: a duty of care, better business disruption measures, and easier use of proactive technology.

turns.speaker: Lord Tarassenko
turns.text: What single change to the Act would make the greatest difference?

turns.speaker: Mark Bunting
turns.text: A duty of care concept to pressure companies to address all identified risks, with comprehensive engagement on risk management. It needs careful thinking alongside the existing regime.

turns.speaker: Suzanne Cater
turns.text: Amendments to business disruption measures to make them more practical. They're our strongest enforcement tool, but we've faced challenges deploying them.

turns.speaker: Oliver Griffiths
turns.text: Make it easier to force companies to use proactive technology to control content served to users. It's narrow but would make a big difference.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thank you. We've had useful discussions. Please write to us with further details on these points.
